summary: Intro discovery focusing on integration patterns (SDK, LangChain/LlamaIndex), gateway/proxy setup, rate limits/quotas, and observability hooks for a potential Hosted -> Dedicated transition. Security and data residency constraints discussed.
topics: Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, data residency
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen (Redwood): Hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro: i'm Maya, account exec on infra team. with me is Carlos Rivera, our solutions engineer. how are you all?
[00:06] Sasha Patel (Lyra): Hey Maya, good — thanks. Sasha here. we've been evaluating a few inference platforms and want to understand integration effort.
[00:12] Carlos Rivera (Redwood): Great. high level today: figure out where you plan to start (hosted vs dedicated), how you plan to call the API (direct SDK, through your gateway/proxy, or via langchain/llama index), and what observability and quota controls you need.
[00:22] Imran Noor (Lyra): Main constraints: latency needs for real-time features (~100-200ms p95), bursty QPS around promotions, and strict data residency rules for EU traffic. also security team will want KMS + audit logs.
[00:32] Jules Becker (Lyra, Security): yes, SOC2 is a must and we use SAML SSO; keys must be in our KMS for private deployments if possible.
[00:38] Maya: Understood. quick question — are you leaning to start hosted for speed of dev or do you need dedicated from day one because of data policies?
[00:44] Sasha: We'd prefer start hosted for dev but we might need dedicated or private in prod. want to see how painful the migration is.
[00:52] Carlos: We do migrations a lot. the API is consistent across Hosted, Dedicated, Private — same SDKs and endpoints with different routing. most customers prototype on hosted and then we help carve out dedicated pools. switching is mostly config + network setup.
[01:01] Imran: can you elaborate on the SDKs? we mostly use python and node microservices and also build LLM chains in LangChain. we also have some narrow search index workflows using LlamaIndex.
[01:10] Carlos: yep. we provide official SDKs for python and node with first-class support for LangChain and LlamaIndex connectors. sample: for langchain you can swap the provider client — there's a Redwood LLM wrapper and a Redwood embedding wrapper. we'll send notebooks. the SDK also has streaming and function calling support.
[01:25] Sasha: is there any extra adapter needed for llama index? we maintain some custom retrieval code.
[01:30] Carlos: LlamaIndex usually plugs in at the retriever layer; you can use our embedding endpoint directly, or run embeddings locally and push to your vector store. we'll provide examples: 1) langchain chain calling Redwood directly, 2) llamaindex using redwood embeddings + custom retriever. both work.
[01:41] Jules: how do you handle auth when requests come from our API gateway? we have an internal proxy that terminates TLS and does JWTs.
[01:48] Maya: you can either call Redwood directly from your backend services with our SDKs using per-service API keys, or use a gateway/proxy pattern. if you use a gateway you typically set up a short-lived token exchange or mTLS between your proxy and Redwood. many customers put a sidecar in front of the client to do token rotation.
[02:05] Imran: any reference for gateway config? we run Kong and AWS ALB.
[02:09] Carlos: we'll share a sample proxy config for nginx/kong and an example of using our token exchange flow. note: if you proxy, be mindful of streaming and websocket fallback; proxies sometimes buffer and break stream semantics.
[02:20] Sasha: good point — we rely on streaming for progressive responses in the product. we can't have proxies that buffer for 30s.
[02:27] Carlos: Right, for streaming we recommend direct service-to-redwood connections or proxy configs that support websocket passthrough. we'll include an example with tangential headers and keepalive settings.
[02:36] Jules: rate limits: how granular are quotas? we need per-service limits and the ability to throttle by route.
[02:42] Maya: Redwood supports account-level and token-level quotas. for Dedicated you can configure per-route quotas and per-api-key rate limits; we also let customers set soft-limits with callback webhooks. quotas can be enforced at the gateway level or by the Redwood control plane.
[02:56] Imran: And throttling behavior — do you reject with 429 or queue? we prefer graceful queuing for user-facing requests up to a point.
[03:03] Carlos: Out of the box we return 429 for excess requests, but Dedicated customers can configure request queuing/buffering windows and burst capacity. there's also an auto-burst policy we can enable for short spikes, with clear SLAs on tail latency.
[03:14] Sasha: observability: we need distributed tracing and token-level cost breakdown so product can map spend to features.
[03:21] Carlos: We have tracing hooks — you can inject trace ids and we propagate them in logs. Console provides token-level breakdown, per-route dashboards, and span links for top slow requests. For higher retention or custom observability we can stream logs to your syslog/CloudWatch/Splunk.
[03:36] Jules: audit logs — retention requirements vary, we may want log exports to our SIEM and kms-managed event encryption.
[03:43] Maya: yes, audit logs export is available; for Private you can host the control plane and keep logs within your VPC, and we support KMS/HSM integrations for key management.
[03:53] Imran: curious about caching and KV — we have a lot of prefix reuse in prompts, can Redwood do prefix/KV caching?
[03:59] Carlos: Absolutely — we do prefix K V cache and automatic prefix detection in the runtime. caching is transparent for supported models and greatly reduces token counts. there's also a configurable TTL and cache invalidation APIs if your data changes.
[04:12] Sasha: model versions: we need to pin model versions for reproducibility in experiments. how does that work?
[04:16] Carlos: You can pin model versions via the control plane, and we expose a versioned endpoint. for Dedicated we can also keep older model variants available as a fallback. rollouts support canary and A/B.
[04:26] Jules: compliance: one more time — SOC2, ISO, SSO/SAML, external pen test reports?
[04:31] Maya: we have SOC2 Type II, ISO27001 artifacts we can share under NDA, and a security whitepaper plus penetration test summaries. SAML SSO for the console and RBAC for team controls are supported.
[04:42] Imran: performance — do you have benchmark numbers for p95 on the 2k token context for the models you host?
[04:48] Carlos: We'll share our benchmark sheet but TL;DR: on Dedicated with a pinned model and optimized kernels you can expect significantly lower p95 vs shared hosted. exact numbers depend on model size and batch settings. also quantization profiles can be recommended by Redwood Optimize.
[05:03] Sasha: how invasive is moving to Dedicated? network wise for VPC peering or private link?
[05:08] Maya: For Dedicated we do VPC peering or PrivateLink depending on cloud. there's a brief networking window for setup; we have runbooks and a project manager for the migration. for Private (on-prem) it's more involved — you get the control plane locally and keys in your KMS.
[05:22] Jules: data residency — can we restrict EU calls to EU regions?
[05:26] Carlos: Yes, routing policies let you pin requests by region or tenant, and fallback to other regions if a hard constraint isn't met. For sensitive data we recommend Dedicated or Private in-region.
[05:36] Sasha: on cost — curious about token-based billing and how caching affects billable tokens.
[05:41] Maya: Billing is token-based on Hosted; for Dedicated you get committed throughput/slots plus overage billing. caching reduces billable tokens because prefix tokens served from cache aren't billed as generated by the model in many configurations — we'll include specifics in the pricing doc.
[05:55] Imran: want to see an example how langchain integration looks in our codebase.
[05:58] Carlos: We'll send a small repo with a langchain chain that uses Redwood as the LLM provider and a llamaindex example for embeddings and retrieval. it includes token counting helpers and a local proxy sample.
[06:10] Sasha: timeline: if things look good we want a pilot in october, low scale, we'll run some benchmarks and decide on Dedicated by end of q4.
[06:17] Maya: that's doable. next step we'll exchange docs and schedule the SE deep dive/benchmarks.
[06:22] Jules: thanks. one last Q — do you support per-route fallbacks to open source smaller models if the main model is overloaded?
[06:29] Carlos: yes, routing policies can define model variants and fallback tiers (e.g., smaller open models or quantized variants). we can route to cheaper models automatically under heavy load.
[06:37] Sasha: perfect, that addresses the cost/latency trade-off.
[06:40] Maya: recap of next steps: i'll send pricing and compliance pack; carlos will share integration samples and proxy configs; sasha will send anonymized traffic for the benchmark. we'll schedule the deep dive.
[06:51] Imran: cool, thanks everyone.
[06:53] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up by email. bye.
[06:57] End of recording.
